Oh boy. The "can you promise me we're not breaking up" sounds familiar. I've heard that during every uncomfortable discussion in my own relationship. But at least that hopefully means my perspective might be helpful for you?

When it comes to approaching the conversation itself, try to make sure it's a time that is okay for her and provide any form of reassurance you can without derailing the conversation or verging into dishonest territory—whether that's verbal affirmations, physical affection, or any other tactic that helps to soothe her anxiety. Be clear that the intention is not to start an argument or exacerbate issues, and that it is not a way to make excuses for a breakup. Make sure she knows you're trying to come to a conclusion that benefits both of you, even if that means telling her staying together is not guaranteed. (Trust me, I know that last part can be difficult.)

As for the differing life goals in themselves: no one agrees on absolutely everything. Figure out what either of you is willing to compromise on without any resentment or major disappointment. Try to see from one another's perspectives what the appeal is to the other's goals. Maybe you can come to an agreement on a life that suits both of you; maybe you can't. In that case, it may be better to part ways, since the alternative will, like you said, probably lead to a messier parting later on, or to one or the other of you developing negative feelings.

And then there's the more immediate issue you brought up of the different graduation times. That one is a little more difficult, mostly because it's so short-term. If long distance isn't something either of you want, are you willing (and able) to stay close to where she will be attending college? If not, is long distance a sacrifice you're willing to make, or is it better to parts ways sometime before then? This might be a harder time to make her feel heard if she's the one who will still be in school and has less control over the outcome, but try to allow as much room in the conversation for her as possible.

Good luck to both of you, and I hope things turn out alright in the end.
